To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the neuropathology of tau in the aging primated brain is similar to that in PSP and CBD, and not to that in AD, even in the context of Aβ deposition.

1) extensive amyloid-beta deposition occurs in the aged cynomolgous macaque brain, 2) 4-repeat tau is selectively deposited as pretangles in aged cynomolous monkey neurons, 3) 4-repeat-tau is also deposited as coiled body like structures in oligodengroglia-like astrocytes, and 4, 30–34-kDa AT8- or RD4-positive tau is increased in aged cynomologous monkey brains.
tau pathology in aged cynolomolgus monkeys, a species with a lifespan similar to that of humans, is progressive supranucleaer palsy/corticbasal degeneration-like but not Alzheimer disease- like.

the question whether aging brains of cynomologus monkeys undergo changes that resemble Alzheimer disease (AD) in humans.
the study of the mechanisms that lead to neurodegeneration.
the development of new therapeutic agents for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related neurodegenerative disorders.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
tau pathology in aged cyno monkeys is PSP/CBD- but not AD-like.
the tau pathology in cynomolgus monkey brains is PSP/CBD-like but not AD-like.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the deposition of tau in aged primate brains is not AD-like, but instead is PSP/CBD-like.
the neuropathological hallmarks of AD, i.e., Aβ deposition and tau pathology, can develop independently in the primate brain, and that Aβ deposition does not necessarily precede tau pathology.
